subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Neutron Stars vs. Black Holes
description: A micro-lesson that makes Neutron Stars vs. Black Holes usable.

hook.text: Both form from collapsed stellar cores. The difference? A neutron star stopped collapsing. A black hole didn't.

buildup.text: Below about 3 solar masses, neutron degeneracy pressure halts the collapse. Above that, nothing can stop it.

discovery.text: The dividing line is called the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit—the heaviest a neutron star can be.

twist.text: Some objects fall in a 'mass gap' between the heaviest neutron stars and lightest black holes. Their nature is unclear.

climax.text: LIGO detected mergers that may involve mass-gap objects—challenging our clean dividing line.

punchline.text: Same death, different outcomes. A few solar masses decide everything.

quiz.question: What determines whether a collapsed core becomes a neutron star or a black hole?
options: The mass of the core—above about 3 solar masses, nothing can stop the collapse
The spin rate of the original star
The temperature of the supernova explosion

details.summary: Neutron stars and black holes are both remnants of massive star deaths, separated by a mass threshold around 2.5-3 solar masses. Neutron stars are incredibly dense (a teaspoon weighs a billion tons) but still have a surface.
details.whyItMatters: The boundary between neutron stars and black holes marks the ultimate limit of matter's ability to resist gravity. Understanding this boundary probes nuclear physics under the most extreme conditions possible.
takeaways: Both form from collapsed massive stars, separated by mass
Neutron stars have surfaces; black holes do not
The dividing line is around 2.5-3 solar masses

faq.question: What determines whether a star becomes a neutron star or black hole?
faq.answer: The mass of the collapsing core. Below about 2.5-3 solar masses, neutron degeneracy pressure halts collapse at a neutron star. Above this limit (the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit), no known force prevents further collapse to a black hole.

faq.question: Could something exist between neutron stars and black holes?
faq.answer: Hypothetically, quark stars (where neutrons break into quarks) could exist just above neutron star densities. Some unusual objects have been detected in the 2-5 solar mass range that don't clearly fit either category.
